heading: Go waits for a real Yon endpoint
summary: A Go service gets its HTTPClient with `// @Needs` above a field such as `greetingClient *GreetingClient`, and calls it like any Go function: `greeting, err := service.greetingClient.Read()`. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own goroutine, so the call waits for the server while the page keeps working; a method that waits returns a promise to the page. `GreetingSetup` adds no adapter, so the request goes to the server of the page: the same origin, without cookies. The answer is read into the `Greeting` model from `client/models` with its `json` tags, and a request body model is written with them as `encoding/json` writes it: `omitempty` leaves out an empty string or a nil pointer instead of sending `""` or `null`, `omitzero` leaves out a zero value (an `IsZero` method decides when there is one), `string` sends a number or a bool as text, and `json:"-"` leaves the field out; an answer of another shape gives an error whose code is `HTTP_RESPONSE`, and a failed request gives the code of the browser transport, such as `HTTP_STATUS`; `BehaviorErrorStatus(err)` gives the status number of an `HTTP_STATUS` answer, such as 404. `Cached` lets the browser cache answer a read, and after a successful `ClearCache` the next read asks the server again. `OverrideSetup` gives `OverrideClient` its own adapter, and that adapter answers instead of the network. Removing the component or leaving the page cancels the request: the page stops the service at once and runs its `OnStop`, the method gets the error code `CANCELLED` afterwards, and a call the method makes after that also gets `CANCELLED` without reaching the server. A getter, a setter or an `OnStart` method cannot wait for the server: the call fails with `HTTP_REQUEST`. A test unit has no browser transport (`HTTP_MISSING`). In a test, `test.construct(service)` fills the `Needs` fields from the `// @Fake` fields of the test; an empty Fake client field gets a client made with `NewGreetingClientWith`, so the TestSetup adapter answers. The server half of this example is a plain JavaScript controller. A controller in TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Go, Dart, Ruby, Lua or C++ answers in the same way (see Controllers), so this section shows only the browser side in other languages.
